clue.text: Fire that awful person taking pictures (3,5)

indicators.note: an awful version of the letters is a mangled one

explanation.surface: Someone wants a dreadful photographer sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'taking pictures' a camera hobby; the definition means stealing paintings, and 'Fire' is not an order but letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: An art thief takes pictures in the sense of stealing paintings.

clue.text: A charming view that can’t be seen in square for example (5,5)

definitions.text: that can’t be seen in square for example
definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for the thing a square lacks; the answer is a noun

blocks.note: an angle is a point of view

explanation.surface: A lovely vista that stays hidden from a town square.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Square' reads as a town square with a view; it is the four-sided shape, all of whose corners are right angles, so it has no acute one.
explanation.definitionFit: An acute angle is under 90 degrees, and a square has only 90-degree corners.

clue.text: Time VCR editor worked to become programme maker (2,8)

indicators.note: worked letters have been worked over into a new shape

blocks.note: T = time, as in physics formulas

explanation.surface: Someone who once edited VCR tapes graduates to making shows.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a career story in television; 'VCR editor' looks like a job title but is just nine letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain job title: the director is the person in charge of making a television programme.

clue.text: Quite resilient comic author (5)

blocks.note: robust, able to survive harsh conditions, as plants are
a surname shared by Oliver of Laurel and ___ and Thomas the novelist

explanation.surface: A funny writer who takes knocks well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comic author' reads as one funny writer, but it names two different Hardys: Oliver of Laurel and Hardy, and Thomas the novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: a robust plant is resilient, and the surname belongs to both a famous film comic and the author of Tess of the d'Urbervilles.

clue.text: Reconstruction of Paris letting gets very noisy (3,9)

indicators.note: a reconstruction rebuilds the letters in a new order

explanation.surface: Building work on Parisian rental flats is making a racket.
explanation.walkthrough: Building works in a city really are ear-splitting, so the surface tells the truth about the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ear-splitting means loud enough to hurt the ears.

clue.text: A craving to be settled (6)

explanation.surface: A strong desire that needs satisfying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settled' reads as a craving being satisfied; it means decided, as in a price both sides have accepted.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of decided: a price that is settled has been accepted by both sides.

clue.text: Taking one’s time reversing difficult racing conditions (5,4)

indicators.note: swaps the two words of the phrase round

blocks.note: heavy ground at a racecourse, which makes for a sluggish race

explanation.surface: Someone dawdles by backing away from a sticky racetrack.
explanation.walkthrough: This turns round whole words, not letters. In British horse racing the 'going' is the official description of the ground, and soft, heavy ground is called slow.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for moving or acting unhurriedly, the same idea as taking one's time.

clue.text: Preachings contain something that’s for everyone (4)

indicators.note: the word holds the answer inside it

blocks.note: the answer sits inside, starting at the third letter

explanation.surface: Sermons carry a message for all.
explanation.walkthrough: Preachings holds pr-EACH-ings; the surface is a sermon with a universal message, which hides that the word is only a container of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Five pounds each' means five pounds for everyone.

clue.text: Something not working with English chap (4)

blocks.note: a dud is something that fails to work, like a dud bulb

explanation.surface: A broken gadget belonging to an English fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Something not working' reads like a vague definition, but it is the first piece, and the one-word definition waits at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal, originally American slang for a man, matching the British 'chap'.

clue.text: Type of service frowned on in hairy location (8)

blocks.note: a serve or bowl delivered with the hand below the shoulder, legal but thought unsporting

explanation.surface: Bad service disapproved of in some scruffy venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service' reads as waiting on tables; it is a tennis serve, and an underarm serve is legal but looked down on.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: an underarm serve is a type of tennis service, and the underarm is the armpit, a hairy spot.

clue.text: Cringed, having bought drinks for about a hundred (6)

indicators.note: the outer word goes about, around, the inner letter

blocks.note: to wine someone is to buy them drinks, as in wined and dined

explanation.surface: Someone flinched after footing the bar bill for a hundred people.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the flinch a reaction to the cost, which is the best part of the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe a small involuntary recoil in pain or embarrassment.

clue.text: Food often seen walking around farm (4,8)

definitions.text: Food often seen walking around farm

blocks.note: the surface wants a whole farm animal raised for meat; the setter means one cut, a dish of feet
not the animal strolling about but the parts it walks on, which are trotting all day

explanation.surface: Livestock wandering the farmyard.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue sounds like it means a whole animal; it is the feet, which are both walked on and eaten.
explanation.definitionFit: Pigs' feet are a traditional dish, and they are also the parts that carry the pig about the farm.

clue.text: Player rings around when season is just starting (5,6)

indicators.note: letters thrown around end up in a new order

explanation.surface: A sportsman phones round as the new season begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' reads as ringing round, and 'season' as a sports season; it is the season of the year.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the first weeks of spring are when that season is just beginning.

clue.text: Proving position is not right (7,3)

blocks.note: a bearing fixes a position or direction
out = wrong, as in 'your sums are out'

explanation.surface: A statement that a stance is mistaken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Position' reads as a stance or opinion, but here it is a compass bearing, and 'not right' means mistaken.
explanation.definitionFit: Bear out is a phrasal verb meaning to support or confirm a claim, which is what proving it does.

clue.text: They help stand a tent that’s knocked over (10)

indicators.note: letters knocked over land in a different order

explanation.surface: Helpers put a tent back up after it blew down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand' reads as a verb with 'help'; it is only letters, and 'They help' is the whole definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by function: attendants are people whose job is to help or serve others.

clue.text: Refusal to take a check for tortilla (5)

definitions.note: a nacho is a piece of tortilla chip

indicators.note: the outer word takes the letters into itself

explanation.surface: A restaurant declines to accept a cheque for a Mexican dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Check' reads as a bill or a cheque; it is the chess term, abbreviated CH.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose definition by material: a nacho is a crisp wedge of fried tortilla.

clue.text: Getting credit for touching report (2,7)

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase for buying on credit

blocks.note: an account is a report of events

explanation.surface: Being praised for a moving news story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Credit' and 'touching report' read as praise for moving journalism; the definition means buying now and paying later.
explanation.definitionFit: A commercial idiom: goods had this way are charged to your tab and paid for later, which is getting credit.

clue.text: Abusive about Victor being broke (9)

indicators.note: the outer word goes about the inner letter

blocks.note: V = Victor in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone is rude about a man called Victor having no money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Victor' looks like a person's name; it is the radio code word for V.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal synonym: someone unable to pay their debts is, informally, broke.

clue.text: Take care of appearance at later stage (4,5)

explanation.surface: Advice to sort out your looks some time later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appearance' and 'at later stage' each give one plain word, and together they make a phrasal verb with a meaning neither has alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain phrasal-verb synonym: minding a child or a house is taking care of it.

clue.text: We often report substandard electrical leads – that’s not so good (5)

indicators.note: the leading letters, the ones out in front

blocks.note: the first letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: An inspector keeps reporting shoddy electrical cables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Electrical leads' reads as cables, which makes 'leads' look like part of the scene rather than the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of bad, so a thing described this way falls short of another, not so good as it.

clue.text: Forced criminals to get educated (11)

explanation.surface: Prisoners are compelled to take classes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminals' is the slang word for convicts, and the surface of prisoners made to study is apt because the answer means exactly that compulsion.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone compelled or obliged to act has been forced.

clue.text: Valuer calls regularly in relation to hearing (5)

indicators.note: take letters at regular intervals, every second one

explanation.surface: An assessor phones in about a hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearing' suggests a court hearing; it means the sense of hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Aural means relating to the ear or hearing.

clue.text: First class date passed without trouble (4)

explanation.surface: A top-notch evening out went smoothly.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a romantic date that went well; 'First class' is ACE, not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To ace a test is to pass it easily.

clue.text: Skirt that essentially limits riding (4)

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its middle

explanation.surface: A skirt whose cut makes horse riding awkward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Limits' reads as a verb about restricting riding; it is just one of two words whose centres are taken.
explanation.definitionFit: A midi is a mid-calf-length skirt.

clue.text: In bed, I use less energy for sex (6)

indicators.note: puts the letter inside the next word
'less' means without, so 'use less energy' is USE without E, the physics symbol for energy

blocks.note: a cot is a small bed
used as printed, placed inside COT to make COIT
USE minus E, the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A tired partner saving energy between the sheets.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a sly bedroom joke; 'In bed, I' tells you to put I into a word for bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Coitus is the formal word for sexual intercourse.

clue.text: Exhaust broken by stick (4,4)

indicators.note: puts one piece beside the other

blocks.note: wear = stick, put up with, as in 'the boss won't wear it'
down = not working, as in 'the system is down'

explanation.surface: A car's exhaust pipe smashed by a stick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exhaust' reads as a car part; it is the verb to tire out. 'By' only sets the pieces side by side, and the answer takes them in the other order.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrasal verb for tiring someone out by steady pressure, the sense of exhaust as a verb.

clue.text: Delicacy is not commonly available in dingy housing (6)

indicators.note: common, non-standard speech
puts the letters inside the next part
the outside shell of the word, its first and last letters

blocks.note: ain't = is not in casual speech, placed inside D…Y

explanation.surface: A fancy dish can't be had in shabby lodgings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Housing' reads as accommodation; it asks for the shell of DINGY. A dainty is an old word for a delicacy, a choice titbit.
explanation.definitionFit: A dainty is a small, choice item of food, a delicacy.

clue.text: Identifies aisles to change (8)

indicators.note: the letters change places

explanation.surface: Someone spots which supermarket aisles need rearranging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To change' reads as 'in order to change', but the 'to' belongs to the letters being rearranged and only 'change' is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To isolate a cause is to identify it.
